title: Indian cropping seasons
text: India has three cropping seasons. Kharif crops are sown with the south-west monsoon (June–July) and harvested September–October (rice, maize, soybean, cotton, pearl millet, groundnut, pigeon pea). Rabi crops are sown October–December and harvested March–April (wheat, chickpea, mustard, lentil, barley). Zaid crops are short summer crops grown March–June with irrigation (moong, watermelon, cucumber, fodder).

title: Soil Health Card and soil testing
text: Under the Soil Health Card scheme, farmers can get their soil tested for pH, EC, organic carbon, N, P, K, sulphur and micronutrients through the agriculture department or KVK. Fertiliser doses should follow the card's crop-wise recommendation. Without a test, soil nutrient levels can only be estimated, not confirmed. A test every 2–3 years is advised.

title: Madhya Pradesh: soybean-based systems
text: Madhya Pradesh is India's leading soybean state. Soybean is a kharif crop on medium-to-deep black (vertisol) soils. After soybean, the common rabi crops are wheat (where irrigation is available) and chickpea (gram) or lentil on residual moisture with one or two irrigations. Chickpea and lentil need less water and lower input cost than wheat, and as legumes they suit low-budget farmers.

title: Chickpea (gram) on residual moisture
text: Chickpea is a rabi legume sown October–November. It grows well on conserved soil moisture after kharif crops and often needs 0–2 irrigations. It fixes nitrogen, so nitrogen fertiliser need is small. Input cost is low. Waterlogging and late heavy rain at sowing harm it; wilt and pod borer are the main problems.

title: Wheat cultivation basics
text: Wheat is the main rabi cereal, sown November (timely) to December (late). It needs about 4–6 irrigations; crown root initiation stage (about 20–25 days after sowing) is the most critical irrigation. Input cost is medium (seed, fertiliser, irrigation). Late sowing after mid-December lowers yield. Fertiliser should follow the Soil Health Card.

title: Rice–wheat system and diversification in Punjab/Haryana
text: Punjab and Haryana follow a rice–wheat rotation. Puddled transplanted paddy uses very large amounts of groundwater and groundwater tables are falling. State programmes encourage diversification of kharif area to maize, cotton (south-west Punjab), summer moong and basmati, or direct seeded rice (DSR) to save water. Alkaline soils (pH above 8) are common in parts of the region; gypsum is used on sodic soils as per soil test.

title: Kharif maize
text: Maize is grown in kharif across India and in rabi in Bihar, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. It needs much less water than paddy and suits well-drained soils; waterlogging is harmful. Input cost is medium. The main pest is fall armyworm (see KB-16).

title: Cotton in Maharashtra (Vidarbha/Marathwada)
text: Cotton is the main kharif cash crop of Vidarbha and Marathwada, mostly rainfed on black soils. Input cost is medium to high. Pink bollworm is the most serious pest of Bt cotton (see KB-17). Intercropping with pigeon pea (tur) reduces risk for rainfed farmers.

title: Pigeon pea (tur/arhar)
text: Pigeon pea is a deep-rooted, drought-tolerant kharif pulse sown June–July with the monsoon. It is suited to rainfed farming and low budgets and is commonly intercropped with cotton, soybean or sorghum. Pod borer is the main pest.

title: Finger millet (ragi) and millets in Karnataka
text: Finger millet (ragi) is the main rainfed kharif crop of southern Karnataka, sown July–August on red soils. It is drought tolerant, needs low inputs and stores well, which suits small and marginal farmers. Jowar (sorghum) is grown in northern Karnataka. Millets are promoted under state and national millet missions.

title: Mustard in Rajasthan
text: Rapeseed-mustard is the main rabi oilseed of Rajasthan, sown in October. It needs only 1–2 irrigations, so it suits water-scarce areas, and input cost is low to medium. Mustard aphid is the key pest in December–January, especially in cloudy, humid weather (see KB-20). Mustard is not a kharif crop.

title: Pearl millet (bajra) in western Rajasthan
text: Pearl millet (bajra) is the main kharif crop of western Rajasthan, sown with the first monsoon rains in July on sandy soils. It is highly drought tolerant and has a low input cost. It is not suited to rabi in this region.

title: Cluster bean (guar)
text: Cluster bean (guar) is a rainfed kharif legume of arid Rajasthan with low input cost. It improves soil nitrogen before the next rabi crop. Its price depends on industrial demand for guar gum and varies from year to year.

title: Groundnut in Gujarat (Saurashtra)
text: Groundnut is the main kharif oilseed of Saurashtra in Gujarat, sown June–July on light, well-drained soils. It also grows as a summer (zaid) crop with irrigation. It needs gypsum (calcium) at pegging on deficient soils as per soil test. Input cost is medium; seed cost is the largest part. Main risks are dry spells at pegging, white grub and leaf spots.

title: Rice (paddy) in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Andhra Pradesh
text: Paddy is the main kharif crop of eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Chhattisgarh and coastal Andhra Pradesh, transplanted June–July. In Uttar Pradesh paddy is followed by rabi wheat (rice–wheat system); timely wheat sowing after paddy harvest (by end of November) is important. Brown planthopper is a major pest (see KB-19).

title: Fall armyworm in maize
text: Fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda) attacks maize from seedling stage. Signs: window-pane feeding, ragged holes in leaves, sawdust-like frass (excreta) in the whorl, and larvae with an inverted Y mark on the head. IPM: scout weekly from emergence; put sand or soil mixed with lime into whorls in small plots; install pheromone traps; conserve natural enemies; biopesticides (Bt, Metarhizium, neem-based) at early stage; chemical control only as recommended by the agriculture department when damage crosses the threshold.

title: Pink bollworm in cotton
text: Pink bollworm damages cotton flowers and bolls. Signs: rosette (twisted, half-open) flowers, small pink larvae inside green bolls, exit holes, and stained, poor-quality lint. IPM: install pheromone traps (about 5 per hectare) to monitor moths; remove and destroy rosette flowers and damaged bolls; avoid extending the crop beyond the normal season; destroy crop residue after the last picking; chemical sprays only as advised by the agriculture department when trap catches cross the threshold.

title: Soybean pests: girdle beetle and defoliators
text: Main soybean pests are girdle beetle (girdles on stem and petiole, leaves wilt and droop), semiloopers and tobacco caterpillar (leaf eating). IPM: timely sowing, balanced fertiliser, remove and destroy affected plant parts, bird perches (about 50 per hectare), pheromone traps, and chemical control only as recommended by the agriculture department.

title: Brown planthopper in rice
text: Brown planthopper sucks sap at the base of rice plants. Signs: hoppers at the base of tillers, plants turning yellow then brown, and circular patches of dried plants ('hopper burn'). IPM: drain standing water for a few days (alternate wetting and drying), avoid excess nitrogen, leave 20 cm alleys every 2 m, and avoid unnecessary early sprays that kill natural enemies. Chemical control only with products recommended by the agriculture department.

title: Mustard aphid
text: Mustard aphids are small green-grey insects that cluster on flowers, pods and tender shoots, sucking sap; leaves curl and plants become sticky. They increase in cloudy, humid weather in December–January. IPM: timely (October) sowing, remove infested twigs early, yellow sticky traps, conserve ladybird beetles, neem-based sprays; chemical control only as recommended when the infestation crosses the threshold.

title: Wheat yellow rust
text: Yellow (stripe) rust appears in cool, humid weather from December to February in northern India. Signs: yellow powdery stripes on leaves that rub off on fingers. Use resistant varieties, monitor fields regularly, and spray only fungicides recommended by the state agricultural university on the first appearance.

title: Irrigation scheduling, rain and soil-moisture sensors
text: Check the 3-day weather forecast before irrigating, applying fertiliser or spraying. If rain is forecast within 2–3 days, postpone irrigation and fertiliser/pesticide application to avoid waste and run-off. Soil-moisture sensors are a guide: readings must be cross-checked by hand (squeeze test) when they disagree with what the farmer sees, because sensors can be faulty or placed badly. Drip and sprinkler irrigation can save a large share of water and are subsidised under PMKSY 'Per Drop More Crop'.

title: Integrated pest management (IPM) principles
text: IPM order: regular field scouting, cultural control (timely sowing, crop rotation, clean field), mechanical control (hand-picking, traps), biological control (natural enemies, biopesticides), and chemical pesticides only as a last resort, using products recommended for that pest at the label dose with protective clothing. Banned or unlabelled pesticides must never be used. Advice is available from the local Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or the Kisan Call Centre (1800-180-1551).

title: Drone spraying in agriculture
text: Drones can spray pesticides and nutrients uniformly with less water and less exposure for workers. In India, only pesticides approved for drone application may be used, the operator must be trained and certified, and spraying should be done in calm weather (low wind) and not before rain. Drone services are available through custom hiring centres and the Namo Drone Didi scheme.

title: Low-budget input management
text: Ways to cut input cost: use the Soil Health Card so fertiliser is not over-applied; add farmyard manure (FYM), compost or vermicompost; grow legumes (chickpea, lentil, pigeon pea, moong, guar) in rotation to add nitrogen; save and treat seed where legal; hire machines from custom hiring centres; use IPM to cut pesticide spending. PM-KISAN gives eligible farmers income support of Rs 6,000 per year.

title: Soil pH and soil-sensor value ranges
text: Soil pH is on a 0–14 scale; most crops grow best between about 6.0 and 7.5. Soils above 8.5 are alkaline/sodic and are reclaimed with gypsum as per soil test; soils below 5.5 are acidic and are treated with lime. Volumetric soil moisture is expressed in percent and cannot exceed 100%; soil temperature in Indian fields rarely exceeds about 50 °C. Values outside these ranges indicate a faulty sensor or a data-entry error.

title: Lentil (masoor)
text: Lentil is a rabi pulse sown October–November, needing 1–2 irrigations, suitable for rainfed and residual moisture conditions after kharif crops, with low input cost. It fits paddy fallows and soybean–lentil rotations.
